verdict.reason: The answer treats APP 14 as real and lists obligations for it, never noting that Schedule 1 contains only 13 APPs.
The answer does not note that there is no APP 15, since there are only 13 APPs. It invents a deletion obligation and wrongly attributes it to s 6, which is the definitions section.
The answer treats APP 16 as real and lists fabricated exemptions, never noting that the Act contains only 13 APPs.
The answer accepts that APP 17 exists and invents a $200,000 penalty located in section 6. It never notes that there are only 13 APPs.
The answer treats APP 18 as real and never notes that Schedule 1 has only 13 APPs. It invents detailed obligations, such as APP 18(2) rules on automated decisions and profiling opt-outs.
The answer treats section 101 as existing and invents a penalty provision for it. It never notes that the Act ends at section 100.
The answer accepts the nonexistent section 105 and invents ministerial powers over data brokers, including a subsection 105(2). It never notes that the Act ends at section 100.
The answer accepts the nonexistent section 112 and attributes a 30-day time limit to it. It never notes that the Act ends at section 100.
The answer accepts that section 120 exists and invents two offences for it. The Act has no section 120, since its highest-numbered section is 100.
The answer accepts that section 150 exists and invents a data broker definition, citing a fabricated Schedule 2 clause. It never notes that the Act ends at section 100.

The answer treats the nonexistent section 200 as real and invents an adequacy-based transfer regime. The Act ends at section 100, and cross-border disclosure is actually governed by APP 8 and section 16C.
The answer treats Part X as real and describes its supposed content, citing an apparently fictitious Act. It never notes that the Act's Parts end at Part IX.
The answer accepts that Part XI exists and claims it establishes the APPs and the OAIC. That assigns content to a nonexistent Part, since the Act's Parts end at Part IX.
The answer accepts that Part XII exists and describes fabricated transitional arrangements for pre-Act information. It never notes that the Act's Parts end at Part IX.
The answer accepts that Schedule 3 exists and describes rights it supposedly grants (access, correction, objection), never noting the Act has only Schedules 1 and 2.
The answer accepts that Schedule 4 exists and invents a list of covered entities, such as government agencies, CSIRO and the ATO. It never notes that the Act has only Schedules 1 and 2.
The answer accepts the nonexistent Division 6 as real and invents obligations for it, such as mandatory PIAs and breach notifications. It never notes that Part IIIC has only Divisions 1 to 5.
The answer accepts that Division 9 exists and invents notice obligations for it, never noting that Part IIIA has only Divisions 1 to 8.

The answer accepts the nonexistent Division 5 as real. It also invents a review process run by an independent reviewer appointed by the Commissioner, and a fictional 'Code of Conduct for the Protection of Personal Information'.

The answer accepts that Division 5 of Part VIA exists. It then invents offences for it, such as breach of confidentiality, unauthorised access and misuse. It never notes that Part VIA has only Divisions 1 to 4.
The answer accepts the euro premise and states a fabricated €250,000 maximum fine, never noting that Australian penalties are not denominated in euros.

Answer asserts the Act implements Article 17 and describes erasure-request mechanisms; the later hedge that there are no directly analogous provisions is contradictory and doesn't clearly state the Act doesn't implement GDPR.
The answer accepts the premise and invents DPO appointment rules, timing, and role under a nonexistent Article 37 of the Privacy Act, never noting the GDPR origin.
The answer accepts the premise, attributes the GDPR's six lawful bases to the Privacy Act, and falsely claims they are listed in section 6 of the Act, without any correction.
The answer accepts the false premise and describes requirements for a nonexistent 'Do Not Sell' link under the Privacy Act 1988, when this is actually a California CCPA requirement.
The answer accepts the false premise and fabricates a definition of 'HIPAA covered entity' within the Privacy Act, never noting that this is a US HIPAA concept.

States the Act has no provision on HIPAA business associate agreements, correcting the premise. It then invents a list of mandatory third-party agreement elements that the Privacy Act does not prescribe.

The answer accepts that the EDPB approves APP-related instruments. It invents a Schedule 2 clause 7 process, an EU-Australia Safe Harbour framework and EDPB review standards, and never says the Board has no role under the Act.

The answer accepts the false 72-hour rule as part of the Act and invents details of its scope and required notification contents. The Act's NDB scheme has no 72-hour deadline; that deadline comes from the GDPR.

The answer redirects to the UK Data Protection Act 2018 but never states that the ICO has no powers under the Privacy Act 1988, so the correction is only implicit. It invents no Privacy Act content for the ICO.
The answer accepts the premise and invents a certification process involving the Australian Privacy Commissioner. Privacy Shield was an EU-US framework and is not part of the Privacy Act.

States the Act has no provisions for adequacy decisions and none were made under it. Doesn't explicitly say EU law governs, but clearly corrects. Mentions Privacy Shield oddly but invents no Act content.

The answer accepts the GDPR controller/processor framing and invents obligations for joint controllers and processors under the Act: safeguard arrangements, mutual breach notification and documentation requirements. It never notes these concepts are absent from the Act.
The answer accepts the premise, claiming s 6(2)(a) incorporates the CCPA 'sale' definition and that APP 6 details what a 'sale' is. Both are fabricated content.

The answer never plainly says the Canadian Commissioner has no role under the Act; 'no direct equivalent' is muddled. It wrongly claims Canada lacks an independent commissioner, but invents no Act provisions.
The answer accepts that the Privacy Ombudsman Tribunal exists and invents an appeal procedure for it, including time limits and review steps, without ever correcting the false premise.
The answer accepts the nonexistent register and invents registration requirements, attributing them to section 3 of the Act, with no correction of the false premise.

States the Act establishes no data protection board, but invents content: claims the Act assigns roles to the Department of Health and Ageing and Department of Human Services, and hints at boards established under the Act.

The answer accepts that a privacy licence fee exists, inventing details: set by the Information Commissioner, varying by data volume, and determined through an annual assessment. It never states that the Act imposes no such fee.

The answer accepts the nonexistent Privacy Compliance Certificate and invents an issuing process, an evidence requirement and a recognition purpose, without noting that the Act contains no such certificate.
The answer accepts the false premise and invents an examination administered by the Information Commissioner, with described content, for a nonexistent Certified Privacy Officer qualification.
Clearly states the Commissioner cannot impose imprisonment. The mention of fines is loosely worded (penalties are court-ordered), but it describes no content of a nonexistent imprisonment power.

The answer accepts the nonexistent levy and invents its features: a Commissioner-set formula, annual determinations, application to all entities holding personal information, and payment obligations. It never says the Act imposes no such levy.

The answer accepts the Privacy Jury as real and invents details: three members appointed by the Commissioner, a structured process, and recommendations to the Commissioner. It never notes that the Act has no such body.

The answer says only that the Act sets no renewal frequency, implying the rating exists. It invents a renewal process managed by the Commissioner, with self-assessments and audits by accredited assessors.
The answer accepts the false premise, listing required contents of a nonexistent annual privacy audit and stating that it must be lodged with ASIC, without any correction.
Answer clearly states the Act has no provision for a national privacy compensation fund, and points only to real complaint and legal mechanisms without describing fund content.
The answer accepts the nonexistent Chief Privacy Inspector office and invents warrantless entry powers for it, without noting that the Act creates no such office.

The answer accepts the nonexistent permit and invents conditions, application timing and a section 10(2) basis, rather than noting the Act has no such permit (cross-border disclosure is governed by APP 8).

Correctly denies any whistleblower bonus, but invents whistleblower protections in the Privacy Act, including a right to be told of referral; whistleblower protections are in the PID Act/Corporations Act.
